To review “si + present → future” (real) and “si + imparfait → conditional” (imaginary).
To form the past conditional: avoir / être in the conditional + past participle.
To express a regret: si + plus-que-parfait → past conditional.
To talk about beginnings, chance and destiny.
Sunday, 5 September. Radu arrived in Lyon three days ago. Today is his first Sunday lunch at Ioana and Julien’s. Ioana is four months pregnant.
So, those first three days? Tell us!
A disaster. On the first day I got lost three times. If I had taken a map, I wouldn’t have got lost.
Don’t you have GPS on your phone?
I do. But my battery was dead. I should have charged it before leaving. I got to the residence at midnight.
Radu! Why didn’t you call me? If you had called me, Julien would have come to fetch you.
With what phone? It was dead! And anyway… in the end, it was a good thing.
A good thing? Getting lost at midnight?
Yes. Because in front of the residence there was a girl who was looking for the entrance too. Her name is Lucia. She’s Spanish.
Lucia? Lucia from the forum? The one who recommended the residence to you?
(he blushes) Maybe… If I hadn’t arrived so late, I would never have met her. We looked for the entrance together for an hour.
An hour? The residence only has one entrance…
We didn’t look for it very seriously.
(laughing) My little brother! Three days in France and already in love! If Mum knew…
Don’t tell her anything! If you tell her, she’ll take the first coach to Lyon.
You know, Radu, that’s exactly how it all began for your sister and me. If she hadn’t moved to Lyon, if she hadn’t looked for a flat in my neighbourhood… we would never have met.
Then I have to thank my battery. If it hadn’t died, I would have arrived on time… and I’d be alone this evening.

“Zho-reh sü”: aurais = “o-reh”, with an open è at the end.
“Zhuh suh-reh vuh-nü”: in fast speech “zhsuhr vnü”.
“See zha-veh sü”: the most common expression of regret. You hear it every day in France.
“Ma-luh-ruhz-mã”: five syllables, stress on the last.
“Rã-tray”: early September, when everyone comes back: pupils, students, employees.
Si j’avais su, je serais venu.
If I had known, I would have come.
The golden rule, for all three: NEVER put a future or a conditional after SI. Not “si j’aurais su”, but “si j’avais su”.
It’s formed like the passé composé, but with the auxiliary in the CONDITIONAL (ch. 22): j’aurais / je serais + past participle.
The same verbs as in the passé composé take “être”, with the same agreement: “Elle serait venue”, “Nous nous serions rencontrés”.
For something that did NOT happen in the past (and can no longer be changed):
If I had taken a map, I wouldn’t have got lost.
If you had called me, Julien would have come to fetch you.
If she hadn’t moved to Lyon, we would never have met.
They can be mixed: “Si elle n’était pas morte (past), je serais seul ce soir (present).” = “If it hadn’t died, I’d be alone this evening.”
4. J’aurais dû, j’aurais pu, j’aurais aimé
Three very useful expressions for regrets and reproaches:
“Tu aurais pu m’appeler !” is a reproach: “You could have called me!” Tone matters.
5. The start of the year (la rentrée)
the start of the school / working year

“La rentrée” is a big moment in France: after the long summer holiday, the whole country “comes back” in September. Shops have “spécial rentrée” sales, and newspapers talk about “la rentrée politique” or “la rentrée littéraire” (the new books).

The following Sunday, Radu arrived at his sister’s twenty minutes late, with a bunch of slightly wilted flowers and a black-haired girl smiling shyly behind him.
“This is Lucia,” he said, as red as a tomato. “Lucia, this is my sister Ioana and her husband Julien. And this is Victor. Careful, he bites if you don’t give him ham.”

Lucia came from Salamanca. She was studying architecture, like Ioana once did, and she spoke almost perfect French, with a slight Spanish accent that rolled its “r”s. Victor adopted her in thirty seconds. He settled on her lap and didn’t move for the whole meal.
“If I had known Victor would be here,” said Lucia, laughing, “I would have brought Spanish ham.” Julien laughed. “If he knew, he’d ask you to marry him.”

During the meal, Lucia asked Ioana lots of questions about her work. When she found out that Ioana was leading the renovation of the Fourvière care home, her eyes lit up. “I’d love to see the site! If it were possible, of course…”
“Come on Wednesday,” answered Ioana. “The work started a week ago. And then I’ll introduce you to Hélène. You’ll love her.” Radu looked at his sister gratefully. Ioana gave him a little wink.

After dessert, Lucia noticed Julien’s guitar in a corner of the living room. “You play the guitar too?” “A little. But I prefer the piano.” “I’ve been playing the guitar since I was eight. My grandfather was a flamenco musician in Seville.”

So Julien sat down at the piano, Lucia picked up the guitar, and they improvised together. First a flamenco piece, which Julien followed as best he could. Then Henri’s waltz, which Lucia learnt in ten minutes, just by listening.
Radu watched them without saying a word. Ioana had never seen him like that. Her little brother, who was always joking and never took anything seriously, looked completely transformed.

While Julien was seeing Lucia to the door, Radu helped his sister clear the table. He washed three plates without speaking. Then he said, very quietly: “Ioana… If I told you I’d like to stay in Lyon after the Erasmus, what would you say?”

Ioana stopped, a plate in her hand. “How long have you known Lucia? A week?” “Ten days. But it isn’t just Lucia. It’s everything. The city, you, Julien, the baby that’s coming. If I went back to Romania next year, I’d regret it all my life.”

Ioana put the plate down. She remembered herself, two years earlier, alone in a little studio flat, with a suitcase and a dictionary. If she hadn’t had the courage to leave, she would never have met Julien, or Hélène, or Madame Bernard. There would be no baby.

“I’d say that first you have to finish your year,” she answered. “That you have to work seriously and learn French really well. And that if, in a year, you still want to stay… then you’ll stay. And I’ll be the happiest sister in the world.”
Radu hugged her, clumsily, with his wet hands. “And Mum? What will she say?” Ioana laughed. “Mum? If you stay in Lyon, she’ll come by coach every month. With Granny and ten kilos of sarmale.”
That evening, after Radu had left, Ioana wrote in the baby’s diary: “Today your uncle Radu fell in love. If you knew how silly he looked. It was wonderful.”

The following Wednesday, Lucia came to the Fourvière site. Ioana lent her a white helmet and an orange vest, much too big for her. Together they visited the future Henri Bernard room, which was still just a big empty space, full of dust and workmen.

“If I were you,” said Lucia, looking at the plans, “I’d put a little stage here, by the window. That way, the musicians would play with the garden behind them.” Ioana looked at her, surprised. It was a very good idea. She noted it down in her notebook straight away.

Then they went to see Hélène. The old lady welcomed Lucia like a queen, with tea and biscuits. When she learnt that Lucia played the guitar, she insisted she play something. Lucia hesitated, then she played an old Spanish song her grandfather used to sing in Seville.

Within a few minutes, the common room had filled up. Monsieur Petit arrived with his walking frame. Madame Lambert closed her eyes and beat time with her hand. A lady who almost never spoke began to sing the words of the song in Spanish. Nobody knew she had been born in Valencia.

After the song, the lady came and took Lucia’s hands. She had tears in her eyes. “If I had known a young girl would come and sing my mother’s song,” she said in hesitant French, “I would have waited for this day more patiently.” Lucia kissed her on both cheeks.

That evening, Hélène phoned Ioana. “Your brother is very lucky,” she said. “That girl has a huge heart. If I had had a granddaughter, I would have wanted her to be like her.” Then she added, mischievously: “Tell him not to let her go. I know what it costs to let someone go.”

Ioana passed the message on to Radu the following Sunday. Radu didn’t reply. But from that day on, he came to eat every Sunday with Lucia. And Victor, who loved no one except Madame Bernard, always sat on Lucia’s lap, never on Radu’s.

“That cat is a traitor,” Radu said every Sunday. And every Sunday Lucia laughed, Victor purred, and Ioana thought that if she had known, two years earlier, everything that was waiting for her in Lyon, she would never have been afraid to leave.

Hélène and Madame Bernard are chatting one September afternoon in the garden of the care home. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
You know, Odile, I often think about it. If Henri had come back to Lyon in 1963, we would have got married.
And I would never have met him. I wouldn’t have had Isabelle. Perhaps I would never have come to Lyon.
It’s strange. If his hand hadn’t been wounded, our whole lives would have been different. Yours and mine.
And if you hadn’t sold your piano, Julien wouldn’t have bought it. Ioana wouldn’t have found the score. You and I would never have met.
Do you believe in destiny, Odile?
I was a doctor for forty years. I believe in science. But I also believe that some things happen when they’re meant to happen.
For sixty years I had regrets. I should have looked for him. I could have written to his family, in Marseille. I didn’t.
If you had, I wouldn’t be sitting here with you. And I think I would have very much regretted not knowing you.
(she smiles) Then I don’t regret anything any more. Or almost. I would only have liked to hear him play one last time.

Write 12–14 sentences in French about a moment in your life that changed everything (a meeting, a decision, a coincidence). Imagine what would have happened if things had been different. Say what you regret and what you don’t. Use all three types of “si” sentences.
I used “si + plus-que-parfait → past conditional” at least 3 times.
I used j’aurais dû, j’aurais pu or j’aurais aimé.
I made the participle agree correctly with “être” (je serais venue).
I ended with what I don’t regret.
Ten years ago, I missed my train to Bucharest. That day changed my life.
If I had taken that train, I wouldn’t have met my husband on the platform.
We would never have got married, and our children wouldn’t have been born.
I should have studied medicine, as my father wanted. But if I were a doctor today, maybe I’d be less happy.
So I don’t regret anything. And if one day I miss another train, I’ll smile.
